text: The basic reason is simple: Saturn's moons, especially Enceladus, might have conditions where life could exist, so NASA wanted to keep the spacecraft away to avoid bringing Earth microbes. Cassini had been flying around the system for over a decade. When fuel ran low, its final orbit was designed to skip Enceladus and Titan, then dive into Saturn. That way it doesn't settle on or near a moon and contaminate it. It's a precaution, because a spacecraft that spent so long in the system could carry trace organisms from Earth. Saturn's thick atmosphere then burns it up, which is the point of the controlled crash.

I'd guess the stationary leg is the one doing most of the holding steady, so it gets a lot of work that people don't think about. On a skateboard, you are constantly making tiny corrections to stop tipping, and that takes real effort from the leg that's planted. If that leg is new to skating, or you're out for a long stretch, the calf, quad, hip or knee can start aching because it's been working hard to stabilize.

From what I've seen, bad stance makes it worse. If your feet are too far apart, you're probably leaning awkwardly and forcing the standing leg to compensate. If they're too close, balance is hard and the leg has to overwork. A slight crouch with knees bent usually helps, and checking your toe angle on the board matters too. Also, if you always push with one side and leave the other stationary, that side can get more fatigue. Beginners often don't realize that simply holding position on a moving board is tiring.

I've noticed people often blame the board or the surface. What's happening is the planted leg is doing more work than the pushing leg. If you mostly push with your right, your left may be the one holding you upright, and over time that side gets more strain.

A few practical things might help: warm up before skating, keep your knees loose, and make sure your shoes aren't too stiff. If the pain is sharp or only in one spot, like just the knee or just the hip, I'd slow down and get someone to check your form, because it may be more than ordinary muscle soreness. But if it's a dull ache after skating, it's likely just fatigue from the balance work, and that usually settles with rest and better stance.

I think the term “Afro-American” is more about ancestry than current nationality. It doesn’t mean most people were born in Africa; it signals African descent, which is historically central to Black Americans’ experience. So the “Afro” part points to that shared heritage, not to a passport.

From what I’ve read, the label also comes from a broader effort to describe identity in a way that recognizes both African roots and American life. That’s why you see variations like “African American” and “Afro-American.” It’s a category, not a claim that everyone traces their family directly to the continent today.

To me, it’s not really a contradiction. A person can be American by birth or residence while still being described as having African ancestry. The name is doing the work of connecting people to a historical lineage, even if the direct link is centuries old.

Honestly, it’s a mix. Smuggling through borders and ports, some local workshops making or modifying things, and old military stockpiles that got looted or handed out. I’d guess a lot of what’s circulating is a patchwork of different generations of gear. And why they still get them? Because there’s no stable ceasefire, and if you’re in a conflict where one side has more guns, you need at least enough to defend yourself. From what I’ve read, the fighting keeps pulling people back into needing weapons, even when they want peace.

Look, I think the short version is that the same brain systems that make you enjoy food, sex, or hanging out with people are also what drugs hijack. When a drug floods the reward pathway with something like dopamine, the brain notices and starts adjusting, which is why tolerance and withdrawal are so common. You're not just getting a bigger signal; you're changing the system's baseline, and that change is where a lot of the downsides come from.

That doesn't mean every drug is "bad" in the same way, though. Some people treat them as if any high is a death sentence, which I think is too sweeping. Opioids, stimulants, alcohol, cannabis and so on hit different systems and carry different risks. A drug that gives intense euphoria is usually doing something pretty extreme to the reward circuitry, and the more extreme the effect, the more the brain has to recalibrate, and the more likely the downsides become.

I've read a lot of opinions claiming there's a perfect drug with zero adverse effects, and honestly that strikes me as wishful thinking. The brain is a feedback machine. If you keep pushing it toward intense pleasure, it will push back. That's not some moral failure; it's just how adaptation works. So even a drug that feels amazing can still leave you needing more to get the same hit, and feeling rough when you stop.

Also worth saying, dose matters a lot. Something can be relatively safe at low doses and a different animal at high ones. The question "why can't there be a drug with 0 adverse effects" kind of assumes we could have maximum reward with no cost, but in practice the cost is built into the very mechanism that makes it work.

So I wouldn't say all drugs are bad. I'd say any drug powerful enough to produce intense pleasure is probably going to have some trade-off, because the brain keeps trying to find a new normal. That's the core of it.

Hi there,

I'm not surprised you said milk. Your brother was basically baiting you with a question where the obvious association is wrong. Cows drink water, but milk is so strongly tied to them that your brain grabbed the first related word. It's a common slip, not you being dumb. I get it too.

I think it's a kind of automatic response. You weren't actually thinking about drinking at all. You were thinking about what cows are known for, and milk just popped out. If he asked again, you'd probably correct yourself to water.

From what I've read, these gotcha questions work because the expected answer is the most obvious related word, not the technically correct one. I mean, he may have been testing whether you'd be fooled by the strong association.

Honestly, that's also the fun of the trick. You don't have to feel bad about it.

Talk soon,

Thanks for asking me about this. Honestly I think the first thing is to work out what you can actually afford, not what you want. I know it feels exciting, but mortgages can sneak up on people. If you can, get pre-approved before you start looking, because that stops you falling for a house you can't get the money for.

I'd also not skip the survey and legal checks. That's the part that saves you from buying into someone else's problems. I mean, you might find something that looks perfect but has issues under the roof, or legal messes around the title. I'd treat that as a must-do, not something to rush through.

And don't get swept up in the house tour. It's easy to fall in love with a kitchen and ignore the rest. Take someone you trust with you, and don't let the seller's enthusiasm do the work for you.

You know, I'm not a lawyer or a mortgage broker, so treat this as a friend's take. If you tell me what you're looking at, I can maybe narrow it down a bit more.

All the best,
Sam

Hey,

Honestly I think the difference is mostly about what you're trying to cover with one product. A 2-in-1 is just shampoo and conditioner in one bottle, so it's still hair-focused. The 3-in-1 adds bodywash to that same formula, which means it's trying to work on both hair and skin.

What I find a little confusing is how they're supposed to do all that in one. The surfactants, conditioning agents and whatever's there for the body all have to coexist in one mixture. From what I've read, the trade-off is usually that none of the jobs gets done as well as a dedicated product would. A real shampoo can focus on cleansing hair, a real conditioner on softening it, and a real bodywash on cleaning skin. The 3-in-1 has to balance all three, so I'd guess the formula has to be milder and a bit more generic.

I wouldn't say it's terrible, but if you care about hair, I'd still use a separate conditioner.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

I keep thinking about this whenever I see the map animation of continents drifting. I'd guess the first thing to say is that they don't just watch the land move in real time. It's too slow for that. From what I've read, the modern way is to put GPS receivers on bedrock and keep measuring the same points over months or years. The positions can change by tiny amounts, and that gives a speed. In practice, the speed comes from measuring the same spots again and again, then working out how much they have moved and dividing by the time between measurements. Satellites add another layer, especially InSAR, which can pick up very small ground movement.

But the old continent-drift evidence still matters too. Matching coastlines, similar rock layers, and fossils on different continents give a longer-term picture. I think the plate speeds are often a few centimetres per year. That feels negligible, until you stretch it over millions of years. And different parts of a continent aren't moving at exactly the same speed, so you're comparing points rather than treating the whole landmass as one block. I'm not an expert on this, but I think the geological evidence is the long baseline, and the GPS is the precise, short-term check. Honestly, it's a mix of careful surveying and a lot of geological argument.

Best,
Alex

Honestly, it comes down to hidden genetic flaws getting exposed. When two relatives have a kid, they share a lot of the same DNA. Because of this, the chance of the child getting two copies of a harmful mutation goes way up. We all carry a few bad genes that don't do anything because you have a healthy copy masking them. But related parents are much more likely to have the same bad genes. When a child inherits the bad copy from both parents, it can mess with brain development. It’s not that the child is born stupid. It’s just that the odds of inheriting two copies of a harmful mutation are significantly higher. This is what we call homozygosity. The more closely related the parents are, the bigger the risk of lower cognitive scores. It’s a pretty brutal piece of genetics, and it’s why we see a real difference in outcomes for inbred offspring compared to the general population.

It’s not really that the arm is special. I think a lot of it is that the arm has more padding, like fat and muscle, so a hit or a shot is spread out over a bigger area instead of landing directly on bone or a nerve. That makes it feel less sharp and urgent. It’s also a place we’re used to using, so our brains tend to downplay it compared with the gut, chest or head. Still, I wouldn’t say the arm always hurts less. A deep cut, a fractured bone, or a wound near a major nerve can still hurt badly, and I’ve heard that being shot in the arm can be pretty rough even if it’s not “the worst”. So the premise is a bit of a myth.

I'd start with what each gas does in your blood, because that's the core of the difference. When you breathe in carbon monoxide, it sticks to the hemoglobin in your red blood cells far more tightly than oxygen does. In fact, I think it binds roughly 200 to 250 times more strongly than oxygen, and once it latches on, it doesn't come off easily. That means your blood can't carry as much oxygen around your body. Your cells start to starve even if you're breathing air that looks completely normal. That's why carbon monoxide is so dangerous: it quietly takes over the oxygen-carrying job.

Carbon dioxide, on the other hand, is something your body produces constantly and you exhale. At the concentrations you normally breathe, it isn't a major threat to oxygen transport. You can breathe elevated CO2 and still feel okay for a while, though very high levels can change your blood chemistry and make you feel drowsy or dizzy. In practice, CO exposure can make you tired, give you a headache, or make you feel like you're getting the flu, which makes it easy to ignore early on. So it's not that CO2 is harmless in every case; it's just that it doesn't hijack hemoglobin the way CO does.

There's another thing that makes CO worse in practice: you can't smell it, see it, or taste it. Carbon dioxide is also nearly odorless, but the real killer is that CO is so much better at grabbing hemoglobin that it beats oxygen in the competition. And because it's so hard to notice, detectors matter. I'd keep one near where you sleep, because that's when you're least likely to get up and escape. That's the main reason it's so poisonous to breathe, while carbon dioxide, at ordinary levels, isn't.

Think of it as getting your body ready for the hit, not as a magic trick. When you brace, you tuck your head down and forward, bring your hands to your feet or cover your face, and tighten your muscles. That matters because in a hard landing or crash, your body keeps moving even after the aircraft stops. Bracing lines up your spine and head with the rest of your body, so the impact force is spread out rather than dumped into your neck or organs. It also helps keep you from slamming into seats, trays, or other passengers.

The reason we teach it is that small differences in posture can change how much force your body absorbs. A tucked head and bent knees mean the shock is shared by your legs and core, with less jarring on your neck. I'd say the position is a simple, practical way to reduce injury, not a guarantee you'll be unharmed. Still, it gives you a better chance of walking away from a bad moment. The crew will tell you when to brace, so listen for that call. It's one of the few things you can control when things go wrong.

I think this is less about businesses not existing and more about what 'well known' means. Before the industrial era, most firms were local workshops, family trades, or merchant houses. They were real, but recognition was personal and regional, not mass media fame.

The industrial era changed that by bringing factories, national distribution, advertising, and standard products, so a name could become known far beyond its home town. Some old firms, like the Dutch East India Company, are remembered as historical institutions, not as brands you'd shop at today. That's why the question is tricky: older firms still exist today.

I keep seeing people brag about those 0% dealer promos and honestly I don’t buy it. My take is that the lower rate is only the headline, not the real price. When I actually ran the numbers on my last car, the bank quote looked worse on paper, but the total came out lower, and that’s what surprised me.

The thing is, dealers often attach those low rates to very narrow conditions: a specific model, a short payoff window, or a required term. Step outside those boxes and the rate jumps. The bank is less theatrical. It usually gives you a flat APR and lets you choose your own term. That flexibility matters, because you can pick a longer payment schedule and keep monthly costs down, whereas the dealer’s cheap rate often forces you into a short loan you might not be able to afford.

There’s also the bundled stuff. I’d guess that a lot of dealer financing quietly adds things like gap insurance or service packages, and those extras can eat up the interest-rate advantage. The bank deal is more transparent: you know the APR, the term, the monthly payment, and what happens if you prepay. That matters more than the advertised number.

I’m not saying banks are always cheaper, and I’m not sure every dealer is shady. But from what I’ve seen, the lower rate is a hook, and the bank’s simpler, more flexible deal often costs less overall. I’d rather pay a slightly higher rate for the freedom to choose a term I can actually manage. That’s the position I’m taking: the real cost isn’t the sticker rate, it’s the total outlay, and the bank tends to win on that.

I keep coming back to how weird it is that marijuana legality in the US is a patchwork of state laws. I think that's more frustrating than the legal status itself. Some states have moved to legal recreational use, others only allow it medically, and a few still treat it as a crime. To me, the bigger issue is that the federal government hasn't caught up. That creates real problems, like when a state-legal sale trips federal rules, or when banks can't reliably serve cannabis businesses. I'd guess the country needs a clearer federal position, not just more state experiments. If a state says it's legal but the feds still call it illegal, that's the contradiction that keeps people confused. I'd want consistency so people aren't navigating two different rulebooks.

I think we’re a bit too quick to say the body “produces electricity,” because it isn’t really sparks or current like a battery. What I mean is that nerve cells move sodium and potassium ions across their membranes, and that movement is what we register as signals. It’s more like charged particles shifting through tiny gates. I’d compare it to a very controlled ion flow, not a flash. I find it less dramatic than people imagine, but still genuinely amazing when you think about how fast those signals travel.

I think a lot of people picture sampling as "steal the whole chorus and make a new song." It's not really that, at least not in the way I see it. From what I've read and what I've heard in studios, sampling is closer to finding one tiny piece of someone else's recording and turning it into something that fits what you're making.

A lot of it starts with digging. Some producers flip through crates of vinyl or search through online archives, looking for that one second of a horn hit, a vocal chop, a drum fill, a piano stab, a synth note. That's the part I find the most interesting, because the value isn't in the song as a whole. It's in the grain of the source. A dusty old recording can have crackle, echo, or an odd resonance that no fresh recording has. So a producer might take a four-bar loop from a 70s soul record, chop it into smaller pieces, reverse a bit of it, layer it under a new beat, and then treat it as a texture rather than a melody.

I'd guess that the practical side is where most of the work happens. You don't just lift a phrase and hope it works. You're matching tempo, pitch, and feel. If the original is 110 BPM and your track is 90 BPM, you have to slow the sample down or time-stretch it, and that can make it sound off. Then there's the legal side, which I think gets ignored too often. Sampling without permission can mean dealing with the original writer and publisher, and sometimes the label too. That's why a lot of people try to keep the sample short, obscure it, or get clearance. But I've also read that even "short" isn't always safe, and that's what makes producers careful.

What surprises me is how much personality comes from the original artist. If I'm making a track and I sample a bit of a 50s jazz solo, I'm not just adding a sound effect. I'm carrying that artist's voice into the new piece. That's the part that makes me like sampling: it's a conversation across time, not just a copy-paste. It lets you build a song that feels connected to something older, but not locked to it.

So if someone asks how musicians sample older songs, I'd say they choose a fragment, break it apart, and rebuild it into their own thing. The old song becomes raw material, not the finished answer. That's the difference between borrowing a moment and stealing a melody, and I think that's where the creativity is.

I think the short answer is that your head isn’t hurting in the way your arm or face hurts. The brain itself doesn’t really feel pain, but the stuff around it does: the membranes, blood vessels, and the trigeminal nerve that runs through the head. So when you get a headache, you’re mostly feeling that outer machinery reacting, not your thoughts or neurons aching. From what I’ve read, a lot of this is the nervous system amplifying signals when things get strained, and tension in the neck and scalp can feed into it. I’d guess that poor posture, not enough sleep, or stress can make those signals louder. It’s a little odd that something as universal as a headache still gets explained with so much hand-waving, but the concrete bit is: the pain is in the coverings and vessels, not the brain itself.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picking this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it’d be easy. We put our names in their totally useless digital waitlist, then were told to come back at 8:23 p.m. to pay. We did, but we stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually said we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15! It was a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn’t completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were even an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and I was surprised there was no line at all. For two people we paid about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be about the same as a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned it actually cost a bit more than what I expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that there was no steak. At that price, I assumed some kind of steak option would be there. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs show up at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, though I didn't try any.

All in all, I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. You hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key repeats now and then too, so "example" comes out as "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught. Honestly, my take is mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good. The circular stage is genuinely smart. You're basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, just that if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats with more clarity.

And honestly, clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like pretty images thrown at me, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also, way too much is happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. A few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Really, just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, I called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my dad. They were never delivered. The sales rep had written down the address wrong, mistaking the “7” in 5407 for a “1,” so they sent them to 5401. The people at 5401 took the package to the local UPS store to have it returned, but it just vanished. We didn’t even find out for weeks. In the meantime, we placed another order for two shirts. Rockmount wouldn’t refund the original pair. The owner took over the dispute. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts came back. He also blamed us a bit for not being friendly enough to the residents at 5401, only four doors away. We fought the original charge with our credit-card company and, after a while, got a credit.
